<meta>continues from previous page</meta>and say to her: "These things, O queen, I willingly suffer for you: you will restore me to wholeness, or certainly you alone are enough for me in place of all else. Cherish me in your pious bosom alone, so that I may not feel the loss of fame, nor even of life itself."

*Sorrow.* I am being torn apart everywhere in the public streets.

*Reason.* Take it in good part. The common crowd will make you known, virtue will make you famous, and conscience will make you secure.

---

### On the shame sought from unworthy praise.
## DIALOGUE XXVI.

> Praise sparingly, for when you praise unjustly,
> If you should later condemn, it will be a mark of levity.
<note>Reason quotes a traditional maxim on the dangers of inconsistent judgment.</note>

*Sorrow.* I am accused of having praised someone unworthy.
<note>A large ornamental initial L begins the response.</note>
*Reason.* I am accused of having praised someone unworthy. An evil that exists often arises from a good root. For the good and innocent believe others to be such as they are themselves. Hence they are even more prone to praise than is just: and although I might admit that praising the unworthy is an evil, yet to vituperate the undeserving is much worse.

*Sorrow.* I have praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* If you did so knowingly, you are blameworthy; but if unknowingly, you are excusable. It is a lesser evil to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is the fault of another; but to deceive is the specific crime of the deceiver.

*Sorrow.* The praise of another turns to my own infamy.

*Reason.* Rather, it is your own fault or ignorance. For as there is no praise from another’s deeds, so there is no infamy.

*Sorrow.* I grieve greatly that I praised an unworthy person.

*Reason.* See to it then that you do not often grieve for that very thing. Beware lest you leap forward rashly to praise or to condemn. For there is a lust for both things: and (to speak accurately) a certain disease and itch of a moving tongue that knows no rest: the bridle and guardianship of which are numbered among the works of extraordinary perfection, as the Scripture says:

<summary>Reason counsels Sorrow on the shame of having praised someone unworthy, arguing that it is better to be accidentally generous in praise than to be maliciously critical. He warns that an undisciplined tongue is a common spiritual ailment that requires careful restraint.</summary>
